decks.title: Chemical Bonding — Part 1: Electrovalent (ionic) bonding
goals: Explain why atoms combine, using the octet and duplet rules
Draw electron dot diagrams for the formation of NaCl, MgCl₂ and CaO
State the conditions that favour an electrovalent bond
Explain the properties of electrovalent compounds

slides.heading: Why do atoms join?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — atoms bond to reach a stable arrangement of electrons like a noble gas. One way is to **transfer** electrons and form ions.

visual.alt: Table of helium, neon and argon with their stable duplet or octet configurations

slides.narration: Namaste! Noble gases hardly react at all, because their outer shells are full: two electrons for helium, eight for neon and argon. Other atoms react so that they too end up with a full outer shell. They can do this by giving and taking electrons, which we study in this part, or by sharing electrons, which comes in Part 2.

slides.heading: Octet rule and the electrovalent bond
slides.body_md: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to get **eight electrons in the outer shell** (an **octet**), or two in the first shell (a **duplet**, as for H, Li). An **electrovalent (ionic) bond** forms when one atom **transfers** electrons to another: the atom that loses electrons becomes a **cation**, the one that gains becomes an **anion**, and the opposite charges attract strongly. The number of electrons lost or gained is the **electrovalency**.

visual.alt: Flow showing a metal atom losing electrons and a non-metal atom gaining them, the ions attracting to form an ionic bond

slides.narration: Atoms try to reach eight electrons in their outer shell, or two if they have only one shell. In an electrovalent bond, a metal atom with only a few outer electrons hands them over to a non-metal atom that needs only a few more. The metal becomes a positive ion and the non-metal a negative ion, and the strong attraction between them is the ionic bond.

slides.heading: Electron dot diagrams: NaCl, MgCl₂ and CaO
slides.body_md: **NaCl:** Na (2, 8, 1) gives 1 electron to Cl (2, 8, 7) → Na⁺ (2, 8) and Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). **MgCl₂:** Mg (2, 8, 2) gives 1 electron to each of 2 Cl atoms → Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻. **CaO:** Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) gives 2 electrons to O (2, 6) → Ca²⁺ (2, 8, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8). Show the metal’s electrons as crosses and the non-metal’s as dots, and put each ion in square brackets with its charge.

slides.narration: Here are the three compounds named in the syllabus. A sodium atom passes its single outer electron to a chlorine atom, so both end up with complete octets. A magnesium atom has two outer electrons, so it needs two chlorine atoms, one for each electron. A calcium atom gives both its outer electrons to one oxygen atom. Crosses show the metal’s electrons and dots the non-metal’s, so you can see where each electron went.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting an ionic formula
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Element X (atomic number 19) reacts with element Y (atomic number 8). (a) Write their configurations. (b) Which loses and which gains electrons, and how many? (c) Write the formula of the compound and its ions.

**(a)** X: 2, 8, 8, 1; Y: 2, 6.

**(b)** X loses 1 electron (→ X⁺); Y gains 2 electrons (→ Y²⁻).

**(c)** Two X⁺ balance one Y²⁻: formula **X₂Y** (potassium oxide, K₂O).

visual.alt: Table predicting the ions and formula of the compound of elements 19 and 8

slides.narration: Start with the configurations. X has one outer electron, which it loses easily, forming a plus one ion. Y has six outer electrons and gains two, forming a minus two ion. The charges must balance, so two X ions are needed for each Y ion, giving X two Y. The real compound is potassium oxide.

slides.heading: When does an electrovalent bond form?
slides.body_md: Electron transfer is easy when one atom has a **low ionisation potential** (loses electrons easily: metals of groups 1 and 2) and the other has a **high electron affinity** (gains electrons readily: non-metals of groups 16 and 17). A **large difference in electronegativity** between the two atoms also favours ionic bonding. So sodium and chlorine bond ionically, but carbon and chlorine share electrons.

visual.alt: Table of three pairs of elements showing that low ionisation potential plus high electron affinity favours an electrovalent bond

slides.narration: An ionic bond forms easily when one atom gives up electrons readily, which means a low ionisation potential, and the other accepts them readily, which means a high electron affinity. Metals on the left of the table and non-metals on the right fit this perfectly. Carbon, in the middle, holds its electrons too tightly to give them away, so it shares them instead.

slides.heading: Properties of electrovalent compounds
slides.body_md: In the solid, ions are held in a regular **crystal lattice** by strong electrostatic forces, so electrovalent compounds are **hard crystalline solids** with **high melting and boiling points** (NaCl melts at 801 °C). They are usually **soluble in water** but **insoluble in organic solvents** such as kerosene. They **do not conduct as solids** (ions fixed in place) but **conduct when molten or in solution**, where the ions are free to move — they **dissociate** into ions, and the current decomposes them (**electrolysis**).

visual.alt: Table of sodium chloride as a solid, melt and solution, showing it conducts only when its ions can move

slides.narration: In a crystal of salt, millions of sodium and chloride ions are locked together by strong attractions, so the crystal is hard and melts only at a very high temperature. Salt dissolves in water, but not in kerosene. Solid salt does not conduct electricity because its ions cannot move. Once it is melted or dissolved, the ions move freely and carry the current, and the compound is broken down by electrolysis.

slides.heading: Worked example: explaining conductivity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Solid magnesium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten magnesium chloride does. (a) Explain. (b) Write the dissociation equation. (c) What happens at the electrodes?

**(a)** In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; in the melt they are free to move to the electrodes.

**(b)** MgCl₂ → Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻.

**(c)** Mg²⁺ ions move to the cathode and Cl⁻ ions to the anode, where they are discharged: the compound is electrolysed into magnesium and chlorine.

nodes.label: Current flows; Mg and Cl₂ formed

visual.alt: Flow from solid magnesium chloride to molten ions that conduct and are electrolysed

slides.narration: A current is simply moving charge. In solid magnesium chloride the ions are held in place, so no charge can move. When it melts, the lattice breaks up into free magnesium ions and chloride ions. The positive ions drift to the cathode and the negative ions to the anode, carrying the current, and there they are converted into magnesium metal and chlorine gas.

slides.heading: Writing formulae from electrovalency
slides.body_md: The electrovalency of an ion is the number of electrons its atom lost or gained. Combine ions so that **total positive charge = total negative charge**.

visual.alt: Table of four cation and anion pairs with the formulae of their compounds

slides.narration: Once you know the charges on the ions, the formula follows. Add ions until the positive and negative charges cancel. Two sodium ions balance one oxide ion. Three magnesium ions, with six positive charges, balance two nitride ions. Two aluminium ions balance three oxide ions.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Atoms bond to reach an octet (or a duplet).
Electrovalent bond: electron transfer from metal to non-metal; ions held by electrostatic attraction.
Favoured by low ionisation potential of one atom and high electron affinity of the other.
NaCl, MgCl₂ and CaO: show crosses for metal electrons, dots for non-metal electrons, brackets and charges.
Electrovalent compounds: hard solids, high melting points, soluble in water, conduct only when molten or dissolved.

visual.alt: Summary table of three ionic compounds and their ions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell. In an electrovalent bond, a metal hands electrons to a non-metal and the ions attract one another. This happens most easily between atoms with a low ionisation potential and atoms with a high electron affinity. Electrovalent compounds are hard, high melting solids that conduct only when their ions can move.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1

Say “ions are free to move” (not “electrons are free”) to explain conduction in the melt.
For MgCl₂, draw two separate chlorine atoms, each receiving one electron.
Check that the charges in a formula add up to zero.

slides.heading: Sharing instead of giving
slides.body_md: Part 2 — when neither atom will give up electrons, they **share** pairs of electrons: the covalent bond.

visual.alt: Table of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen and nitrogen molecules with their numbers of shared pairs

slides.narration: Two chlorine atoms both want one more electron, and neither will give one up. Instead, each puts one electron into a shared pair, and both atoms count that pair as their own. This sharing is a covalent bond. In this part we draw covalent molecules, see why some are polar, and meet a special kind of shared pair called a coordinate bond.

slides.heading: Covalent bonds: single, double and triple
slides.body_md: A **covalent bond** is formed by **sharing a pair of electrons**, each atom contributing one. **H₂:** one shared pair gives each H a duplet. **Cl₂:** one shared pair (single bond) completes both octets. **O₂:** two shared pairs (**double bond**). **N₂:** three shared pairs (**triple bond**). **CH₄:** carbon shares one pair with each of four H atoms. **CCl₄:** the same, with four Cl atoms. Unshared pairs on an atom are **lone pairs**.

slides.narration: In a covalent bond each atom gives one electron to a shared pair. Hydrogen and chlorine molecules share one pair, a single bond. Oxygen atoms need two more electrons each, so they share two pairs, a double bond. Nitrogen atoms share three pairs, a triple bond. In methane, carbon shares a pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, and carbon tetrachloride is the same with four chlorine atoms.

slides.heading: Non-polar molecules
slides.body_md: When two **identical atoms** share a pair (H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂), the pair is shared **equally**: the bond is **non-polar**. CH₄ and CCl₄ contain bonds between different atoms, but the four bonds point symmetrically to the corners of a **tetrahedron**, so their effects **cancel** and the molecules are **non-polar** overall.

visual.alt: Table of chlorine, methane and carbon tetrachloride showing why each molecule is non-polar

slides.narration: If both atoms in a bond are the same, they pull equally on the shared pair, so the bond is non-polar. Methane and carbon tetrachloride are more interesting: each carbon to chlorine bond is slightly uneven, but the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, so their pulls cancel out and the molecule as a whole is non-polar.

slides.heading: Worked example: drawing a covalent molecule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Draw the electron dot structure of carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄, and state the number of shared pairs and lone pairs.

**Step 1.** C (2, 4) has 4 valence electrons; each Cl (2, 8, 7) has 7.

**Step 2.** C shares one pair with each Cl: **4 shared pairs** (single bonds).

**Step 3.** Each Cl keeps 3 lone pairs: **12 lone pairs** in all; carbon has none.

Every atom now has an octet.

visual.alt: Table counting valence electrons, shared pairs and lone pairs in carbon tetrachloride

slides.narration: Carbon has four outer electrons, so it can share one with each of four chlorine atoms. Each chlorine has seven outer electrons; after sharing one pair, it keeps three lone pairs. That gives four shared pairs and twelve lone pairs in total, and every atom ends up with eight electrons around it.

slides.heading: Polar molecules: HCl, H₂O and NH₃
slides.body_md: When two **different atoms** share a pair, the **more electronegative** atom pulls the pair closer and gets a **partial negative charge (δ−)**; the other gets **δ+**. Such a bond is **polar**. **HCl:** Cl is δ−, H is δ+. **H₂O:** O shares two pairs with H atoms and has **two lone pairs**; the molecule is bent and polar. **NH₃:** N shares three pairs and has **one lone pair**; the molecule is pyramidal and polar.

slides.narration: If the two atoms are different, the more electronegative one pulls the shared pair closer and becomes slightly negative, while the other becomes slightly positive. Hydrogen chloride is polar in this way. Water has two lone pairs on oxygen and a bent shape, and ammonia has one lone pair on nitrogen and a pyramid shape, so both molecules are polar.

slides.heading: Covalent compounds compared with electrovalent compounds
slides.body_md: Covalent compounds are made of **molecules** held together only by **weak forces**, so most are gases, liquids or soft solids with **low melting and boiling points**. Most are **insoluble in water** but **soluble in organic solvents**, and they **do not conduct** electricity. Some **polar** covalent compounds such as **HCl** **ionise in water**: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, so hydrochloric acid conducts.

rows: Usually no (except some polar ones in water)

visual.alt: Table comparing electrovalent and covalent compounds in particles, state, melting point, solubility and conductivity

slides.narration: Covalent compounds are made of separate molecules, and the forces between the molecules are weak. That is why many are gases or liquids, with low melting and boiling points. They usually dissolve in organic solvents rather than water and do not conduct. A few polar ones, like hydrogen chloride, react with water to form ions, so their solutions do conduct.

slides.heading: Worked example: classifying from properties
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Substance P melts at 770 °C and conducts when molten. Substance Q boils at −85 °C, does not conduct as a liquid, but its solution in water conducts. Identify the type of bonding in each and explain Q’s behaviour.

**P:** high melting point, conducts when molten → **electrovalent** (for example KCl).

**Q:** very low boiling point, non-conducting liquid → **covalent molecules**. It is **polar** and ionises in water, like HCl: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.

slides.narration: A very high melting point and conduction in the melt point to ions, so P is electrovalent. Q boils far below zero and its liquid does not conduct, so it is made of covalent molecules. Its solution conducts because the polar molecules react with water to form ions, exactly as hydrogen chloride does.

slides.heading: Coordinate bonds: H₃O⁺ and NH₄⁺
slides.body_md: A **lone pair** is a pair of valence electrons not used in bonding. In a **coordinate (dative) bond**, **both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom** (the donor); the acceptor has an empty place. Once formed it is the same as any covalent bond. **H₃O⁺:** a lone pair on the O of water is donated to H⁺: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺. **NH₄⁺:** the lone pair on N of ammonia is donated to H⁺: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺. Water itself contains a few H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ ions, because one water molecule’s lone pair takes H⁺ from another: H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.

slides.narration: A lone pair is a pair of outer electrons that is not used in a bond. In a coordinate bond, one atom supplies both electrons of the shared pair. The oxygen in water has lone pairs, and a hydrogen ion has none at all, so the oxygen donates a lone pair to make the hydronium ion. Ammonia does the same with its lone pair to make the ammonium ion.

notes.title: Chemical Bonding — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Electrovalent (ionic) bonding
sections.body_md:
Atoms combine to reach a noble-gas arrangement: an **octet** (or a **duplet** for the first shell). An **electrovalent bond** is formed by **transfer of electrons** from a metal atom (low ionisation potential) to a non-metal atom (high electron affinity); the ions are held by **electrostatic attraction**. Electrovalency = number of electrons lost or gained.

| Compound | Transfer | Ions |
|---|---|---|
| NaCl | Na (2, 8, 1) → 1 e⁻ → Cl (2, 8, 7) | Na⁺ (2, 8), Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) |
| MgCl₂ | Mg (2, 8, 2) → 1 e⁻ to each of 2 Cl | Mg²⁺, 2Cl⁻ |
| CaO | Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) → 2 e⁻ → O (2, 6) | Ca²⁺, O²⁻ (2, 8) |

In dot diagrams: crosses for the metal’s electrons, dots for the non-metal’s, square brackets and charges on the ions.

key_terms.definition_md: A bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, the resulting ions being held by electrostatic attraction.
The number of electrons an atom loses or gains in forming an ionic bond.

rows: Low ionisation potential of the metal
High electron affinity of the non-metal

visual.alt: Table of the conditions that favour electrovalent bonding

sections.heading: 2. Properties of electrovalent compounds
sections.body_md:
- **Hard crystalline solids**: ions in a lattice held by strong forces.
- **High melting and boiling points** (NaCl melts at 801 °C).
- **Soluble in water**, insoluble in organic solvents (kerosene, petrol).
- **Conduct only when molten or in aqueous solution**: the compound **dissociates** into free ions (NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻), which carry current and are discharged at the electrodes — **electrolysis**. Solid: ions fixed, no conduction.

key_terms.definition_md: The separation of an electrovalent compound into its free ions when melted or dissolved.

visual.alt: Table of sodium chloride conductivity in three states

sections.heading: 3. Covalent bonding: non-polar molecules
sections.body_md:
A **covalent bond** is a **shared pair of electrons**, one electron from each atom. Single bond = 1 pair, double = 2 pairs, triple = 3 pairs. **Lone pairs** are unshared valence pairs.

| Molecule | Shared pairs | Lone pairs |
|---|---|---|
| H₂ | 1 (H–H) | 0 |
| Cl₂ | 1 (Cl–Cl) | 3 on each Cl |
| O₂ | 2 (O=O) | 2 on each O |
| N₂ | 3 (N≡N) | 1 on each N |
| CH₄ | 4 C–H | 0 |
| CCl₄ | 4 C–Cl | 3 on each Cl |

Identical atoms share equally (**non-polar**). CH₄ and CCl₄ are symmetrical (tetrahedral), so they are **non-polar molecules**.

key_terms.definition_md: A bond formed by the sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms, each contributing one electron.
A pair of valence electrons on an atom that is not used in bonding.

visual.alt: Table of single, double and triple bonds with examples

sections.heading: 4. Polar covalent molecules
sections.body_md:
When different atoms share a pair, the **more electronegative** atom attracts it more strongly and carries **δ−**; the other carries **δ+**: a **polar covalent bond**.

- **HCl**: H(δ+)–Cl(δ−); one shared pair, three lone pairs on Cl.
- **H₂O**: two O–H bonds, **two lone pairs** on O; bent; polar.
- **NH₃**: three N–H bonds, **one lone pair** on N; pyramidal; polar.

key_terms.definition_md: A covalent bond in which the shared pair lies closer to the more electronegative atom, giving partial charges.

visual.alt: Table of bond pairs and lone pairs in HCl, water and ammonia

sections.heading: 5. Electrovalent and covalent compounds compared
sections.body_md:
| Property | Electrovalent | Covalent |
|---|---|---|
| Particles | Ions | Molecules |
| State | Hard crystalline solids | Gases, liquids, soft solids |
| Melting / boiling point | High | Low |
| Solubility | Water | Organic solvents |
| Conductivity | Molten or aqueous: yes; solid: no | Non-conductors |

Some polar covalent compounds **ionise in water** and conduct: $\ce{HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Formation of ions when a polar covalent compound such as HCl reacts with water.

visual.alt: Table classifying three substances by bonding

sections.heading: 6. Coordinate bonding
sections.body_md:
A **coordinate (dative) bond** is a shared pair in which **both electrons come from one atom** (the donor, which has a **lone pair**); the acceptor (here H⁺) has none.

- $\ce{H2O + H+ -> H3O+}$ (hydronium ion: 2 covalent + 1 coordinate bond)
- $\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}$ (ammonium ion: 3 covalent + 1 coordinate bond)
- Water self-ionises: $\ce{H2O + H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-}$ — the lone pair on one water molecule takes H⁺ from another.

key_terms.definition_md: A covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.

visual.alt: Table of donor and acceptor in hydronium and ammonium ions

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Drawing inner-shell electrons in dot diagrams, or forgetting brackets and charges on ions.
- Saying solid sodium chloride conducts.
- Drawing O₂ with a single bond or N₂ without lone pairs.
- Calling CCl₄ polar.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Dot diagram (2 marks): correct electrons on each atom, and correct ions or shared pairs.
- Properties (1 mark each): property with the reason (ions fixed or free; weak forces between molecules).
- Coordinate bond (2 marks): lone pair donated, product ion with charge.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by an electrovalent bond? State the conditions that favour its formation. [2]

(b) Draw electron dot diagrams to show the formation of sodium chloride from sodium (11) and chlorine (17). [2]

(c) Element X has atomic number 12 and element Y has atomic number 9. (i) Write their configurations. (ii) Write the formula of the compound XY₂ in terms of ions. (iii) Name the bond. [3]

(d) Give reasons: (i) solid sodium bromide does not conduct but its solution does; (ii) magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride; (iii) sodium chloride dissolves in water but not in petrol. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A bond formed by complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another; the ions are held by electrostatic attraction. Favoured by low ionisation potential of one atom (a metal) and high electron affinity of the other (a non-metal).

(b) Na with one cross in the outer shell; Cl with seven dots; the cross moves to Cl, giving [Na]⁺ and [Cl with seven dots and one cross]⁻ in brackets.

(c) (i) X: 2, 8, 2; Y: 2, 7. (ii) X²⁺(Y⁻)₂ (MgF₂). (iii) Electrovalent.

(d) (i) In the solid the ions are fixed; in solution they are free to move. (ii) Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, so the attraction in MgO is much stronger. (iii) Water attracts and separates the ions; petrol, a non-polar solvent, does not.

questions.solution_md: Definition and conditions; dot diagram; configurations and formula; reasons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a covalent bond? How does a double bond differ from a single bond? [2]

(b) Draw electron dot structures of (i) a nitrogen molecule and (ii) methane. [2]

(c) (i) Name a non-polar molecule that contains polar bonds. (ii) Explain why it is non-polar. (iii) State its shape. [3]

(d) State three properties of covalent compounds such as tetrachloromethane and explain any one of them. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A bond formed by sharing a pair of electrons, one from each atom. A single bond is one shared pair; a double bond is two shared pairs (as in O₂).

(b) (i) N≡N: three shared pairs between the N atoms and one lone pair on each N. (ii) C at the centre sharing one pair with each of four H atoms.

(c) (i) CCl₄ (or CH₄). (ii) The bond polarities cancel because the bonds are arranged symmetrically. (iii) Tetrahedral.

(d) Low melting and boiling points; insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents; do not conduct electricity. Explanation (any one): e.g. low boiling point — only weak forces between molecules have to be overcome.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define electronegativity and explain how a difference in electronegativity makes a covalent bond polar. [2]

(b) Draw the electron dot structure of water and mark the partial charges. [2]

(c) Compare HCl and NaCl with respect to (i) the type of bond, (ii) the particles present in the pure substance and (iii) electrical conductivity of the pure liquid. [3]

(d) Hydrogen chloride gas dissolves in water and the solution turns blue litmus red. (i) Write the equation for the ionisation. (ii) Name the positive ion formed. (iii) Explain why the pure liquid does not conduct but the solution does. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair towards itself. When the two atoms differ, the pair lies closer to the more electronegative atom, which becomes δ− while the other becomes δ+.

(b) O with two shared pairs to two H atoms and two lone pairs; O δ−, each H δ+.

(c) (i) HCl: polar covalent; NaCl: electrovalent. (ii) HCl: molecules; NaCl: ions. (iii) Liquid HCl does not conduct; molten NaCl conducts.

(d) (i) HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻. (ii) Hydronium ion. (iii) Pure liquid HCl contains only molecules; in water it ionises, giving free ions that carry charge.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define (i) a lone pair and (ii) a coordinate bond. [2]

(b) Draw an electron dot diagram for the formation of the hydronium ion from water and a hydrogen ion. [2]

(c) (i) How many lone pairs are present on the nitrogen of ammonia? (ii) Write the equation for the formation of the ammonium ion. (iii) How many coordinate bonds are present in the ammonium ion? [3]

(d) Explain (i) why methane does not form CH₅⁺ in the same way, (ii) why water contains a small number of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ ions, and (iii) why the four N–H bonds of NH₄⁺ cannot be told apart once it has formed. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) A pair of valence electrons on an atom not used in bonding. (ii) A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom.

(b) H₂O with two shared pairs and two lone pairs on O; H⁺ with no electrons; one lone pair of O shared with H⁺, giving [H₃O]⁺ with three shared pairs and one lone pair.

(c) (i) One. (ii) NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺. (iii) One.

(d) (i) Carbon in methane has no lone pair to donate. (ii) A lone pair on one water molecule accepts H⁺ from another: H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻. (iii) Once formed, a coordinate bond is a shared pair just like the others.

questions.stem_md:
Elements P, Q and R have atomic numbers 19, 8 and 1.

(a) Write the electronic configurations of P, Q and R. [2]

(b) (i) Name the type of bond formed between P and Q and write the formula of the compound. (ii) Name the type of bond formed between Q and R and write the formula of the compound. [2]

(c) For the compound of Q and R: (i) state the number of lone pairs on Q, (ii) state whether the molecule is polar, and (iii) name the ion formed when it accepts H⁺. [3]

(d) Predict, with reasons, which of the two compounds in (b) (i) has the higher melting point, (ii) conducts when molten and (iii) dissolves in kerosene. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) P: 2, 8, 8, 1; Q: 2, 6; R: 1.

(b) (i) Electrovalent; P₂Q (K₂O). (ii) Covalent (polar); R₂Q (H₂O).

(c) (i) Two. (ii) Polar. (iii) Hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.

(d) (i) P₂Q — ions held by strong electrostatic forces. (ii) P₂Q — its ions become free to move in the melt; water is molecular. (iii) Neither readily: P₂Q is ionic (insoluble in non-polar solvents) and water is polar and does not mix with kerosene.
